opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it fits in very naturally, even though historically the two fields haven't talked to each other as much as they should have.

Statistics is fundamentally about decision-making under uncertainty. Go back to Wald and statistical decision theory: you have a decision-maker, a loss function, and nature, which is sort of an adversary or at least an unknown. That's already a game. Wald was very aware of von Neumann's work, and minimax is a game-theoretic concept. So in some sense the roots are shared.

What's been missing, especially in machine learning, is the recognition that most of the interesting problems don't involve a single decision-maker. Machine learning has mostly been framed as one agent, maybe a company, sitting with a big pile of data and trying to make good predictions. But in the real world the data come from people, and those people have their own goals and incentives. They respond to the system. They might strategically change their behavior, or decide whether to share their data at all. Once you take that seriously, you're no longer doing pure optimization. You're in a multi-agent setting, and you need equilibrium concepts, mechanism design, incentive compatibility, all the tools economists have developed.

On the other hand, economics and game theory have often assumed agents know their preferences and the relevant probabilities. In reality they don't. They have to learn them from data, often from very little data, and they make errors. That's where statistics comes in. So I see a real blending: learning-aware mechanisms on one side, and incentive-aware learning on the other.

One example I've worked on is what I call statistical contract theory. Think of a regulator like the FDA dealing with pharmaceutical companies. The company knows more about its drug than the regulator does, and the regulator designs a protocol, a hypothesis test, essentially a contract, that determines what happens based on the evidence. The company decides whether to run the trial based on its own private beliefs. If you design the statistical procedure without thinking about those incentives, you can get very bad outcomes. If you think of the test as part of a mechanism, you can design something that works well even though the agents are strategic. That's statistics and game theory together, and neither alone gives you the answer.

More broadly, I think the right way to view a lot of what we call AI isn't as building an imitation of an individual human intelligence, but as building systems, markets really, that link together producers and consumers, data and decisions, at scale. Markets are collectives of agents interacting. To design good ones you need game theory, you need statistics to handle the uncertainty, and you need computer science to make it run at scale. That combination is, I think, the engineering discipline we actually need, and it's where much of my thinking has been heading.

r001.rationale: The candidate says game theory fits naturally into Jordan’s thinking and that multi-agent machine learning requires equilibrium concepts.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I've come to think of it as central, actually, and that's been a shift for me over the years. Classical statistics, going back to Fisher and Neyman and Wald, was built around a very particular picture: there's nature, nature is indifferent, it generates data according to some distribution, and the statistician sits on the other side trying to infer something about it. Wald even framed it as a game, but a game against an adversary who doesn't really care about you. Nature doesn't have preferences.

But if you look at where data actually come from today, that picture is just wrong. Data come from people. They come from markets, from platforms, from other agents who have their own goals, who are responding to what you do, and who will change their behavior when they realize you're learning from them. So the moment you deploy a statistical procedure in the world, the distribution you were estimating is no longer the distribution you're facing. That's not a nuisance to be patched over. That is the problem.

And once you take that seriously, you're in game theory whether you like it or not. You have multiple agents, each with partial information, each learning, each with incentives, and the question becomes: what are the equilibria of that system, and are they any good? That's a very different question from "what's the minimax rate for this estimator."

What I find compelling is that economists had half of the picture and we had the other half. Economics has had this beautiful theory of incentives and mechanisms and equilibria, but historically with very idealized assumptions about information and rationality. Statistics and machine learning have had rich theories of learning from data under uncertainty, but with this naive view of a passive environment. The interesting work is in the middle. Things like designing markets that use data flows as signals, or thinking about how recommendation systems create feedback loops between producers and consumers, or how you share uncertainty across many decision-makers rather than one.

So I'd say the statistician in me hasn't gone away. I still care deeply about uncertainty quantification, about guarantees, about what you can and can't conclude. But I've stopped thinking of the decision-maker as a lone individual. The unit of analysis is the collective, the system of interacting agents, and the goal isn't just prediction accuracy. It's something more like social welfare. And frankly, I think that's where the real intellectual action is going to be for the next few decades, far more than in making any single model a bit more accurate.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls game theory central to his thinking and says the key question is what equilibria arise in systems of interacting agents.

astra-6.text:
As a statistician, I’m used to thinking about uncertainty: I have data, I have a model, and I want to make a decision. But once that decision affects other people, who are also making decisions, the problem changes. Their behavior affects the data I’ll see next. So the environment isn’t simply something fixed that I’m trying to learn about. It responds.

That’s where game theory becomes very natural. It gives us a language for thinking about interacting decision makers, their incentives, and the consequences of their interactions. And statistics brings something essential to that picture, because those decision makers don’t know everything. They have to learn from limited information.

Think about a recommendation system. You’re not just predicting whether somebody will like a song. You’re directing attention toward musicians, affecting their opportunities, and potentially changing what gets produced. There’s a whole system of people participating in that process.

So I’m interested in bringing those perspectives together: learning, uncertainty, incentives, and allocation. Prediction is part of the problem, but we also have to ask what happens when people act on those predictions, and how to design the interactions so that the resulting system works well.

r001.rationale: The response presents game theory as a natural part of thinking about interacting decision makers and incentives, but it does not mention or otherwise identify equilibria as part of Jordan’s thinking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think game theory enters when you stop thinking of a learning system as an isolated entity. In statistics, we often start with a decision-maker who observes data and chooses an action under uncertainty. But in many real systems, there are other decision-makers, and their actions affect the data you see and the consequences of what you do.

Think about a recommendation system. There are users, content creators, advertisers, and a platform. They all have different objectives, and they adapt to one another. So predicting what someone will click is only one small part of the problem. You also have to ask what incentives your system creates and what happens as people respond to those incentives.

That’s where statistics and game theory need each other. Game theory gives us a language for interacting decisions, while statistics brings uncertainty, limited information, and learning into the picture. The interesting question is how to design systems in which those interactions lead to useful outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response presents game theory as useful for analyzing interacting decisions and incentives, but it does not mention equilibria or connect them to Jordan’s thinking.
